item.title: NATO’s War in Ukraine
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
I published the following article in a Norwegian newspaper in February 2023, on the first anniversary of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. My argument is that the war will continue until an agreement can be reached on the European security architecture: Natos krig | Klassekampen

We are constantly told that Russia’s invasion was unprovoked and motivated solely by the desire to annex territory. The conclusion, therefore, is that Moscow cannot be negotiated with and that NATO’s role in the war is solely to help Ukraine defend itself. With such a narrative, we are convinced that there is only a military solution and that Norway therefore had to abandon its tradition of refraining from sending Norwegian weapons to war zones.

But if NATO provoked the war and sabotaged all attempts at peace, then the weapons shipments must be interpreted as a cynical use of Ukrainians in a Cold War against Russia. Acknowledging NATO’s involvement in this war is necessary to begin negotiations, and it should not be equated with supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In 1990, we established a new, inclusive Europe with the “Charter of Paris for a New Europe.” The agreement was based on “indivisible security” and “sovereign equality” in a Europe without dividing lines. Four years later, we developed a common security institution with Russia, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), based on the same principles.

The decision to expand NATO resulted in the principles of these agreements being abandoned. Instead of “indivisible security,” NATO increased its own security at the expense of Russian security. Instead of a Europe without dividing lines, we are fighting a new Cold War over where the new dividing lines should be drawn. Ukraine, Georgia, Belarus, and Moldova are therefore the new front line.

In 1994, even President Clinton warned that NATO expansion could destabilize Europe, as drawing a new line between East and West could create a self-fulfilling prophecy of future confrontation. When Clinton changed his mind, his Secretary of Defense, William Perry, considered resigning in protest. Perry claims that those pushing for NATO expansion acknowledged that it would destroy peace with Russia, but did not believe it mattered because Russia was weak, and their attitude was essentially: “Who cares what they think?”

Jack Matlock, the U.S. ambassador to the Soviet Union who participated in negotiations to end the Cold War, condemned NATO expansionism as a betrayal of Russia that destroyed the foundation for lasting peace. George Kennan, the architect of the containment policy toward the Soviet Union, predicted that NATO expansionism was a provocation that would start a new Cold War, and that if Russia responded to the provocations, NATO would wrongly place all the blame on Russia.

Bringing Ukraine onto our side of the new dividing lines in Europe was a recipe for war. William Burns, the U.S. ambassador to Russia and now CIA director, warned in 2008 that bringing Ukraine into NATO could trigger a civil war and that Russia would likely intervene on behalf of eastern Ukraine, something Moscow did not want to have to do. Angela Merkel agreed with this assessment when she argued that giving Ukraine a Membership Action Plan to join NATO would be interpreted by Moscow as “a declaration of war”.

But NATO continued pushing Ukrainians toward membership they did not want. In 2011, NATO published a report arguing that the greatest challenge in its relationship with Ukraine was that NATO membership was highly unpopular, with some opinion polls showing less than 20 percent support among the population. In 2014, NATO supported a “democratic revolution” that did not have majority support among Ukrainians and that violated the constitution.

Leaked phone calls revealed that the United States had handpicked the new administration several weeks before helping remove the democratically elected president from power.

The civil war predictably began after the coup, and Russia intervened. The conflict appeared to be resolved in February 2015 with the Minsk Agreement, to which all parties—including the West—committed themselves. We have since learned that the United States and Britain sabotaged the peace agreement for seven years, and both Germany and France now claim that the agreement was only created to buy time to arm “their” Ukraine.

In 2019, Zelensky was elected with 73 percent of the vote on a peace platform, promising to implement the Minsk Agreement in order to achieve peace with Donbas and Russia. But he made a complete U-turn after nationalists funded and trained by the United States threatened to kill him.

In 2021, Moscow attempted to negotiate with NATO to stop the increased American presence along its borders, including NATO’s modernization of two Ukrainian ports so that they could be used by American warships. The former head of Russia analysis at the CIA argued in December 2021 that Russia could invade because “the risk of inaction” had become too great.

Russia invaded in February 2022 to establish a new status quo in Ukraine after eight years of war in Donbas and NATO’s gradual buildup of the Ukrainian military.

Three days into the invasion, negotiations had already begun. Israeli Prime Minister Bennett mediated in the negotiations and claims that both Russia and Ukraine wanted an agreement under which Ukraine would stay out of NATO in exchange for Russia withdrawing its forces. But according to Bennett, the United States and Britain sabotaged the peace agreement because they wanted to use the Ukrainian army they had built against Russia. Turkey’s Foreign Minister also confirmed the two parties came close to an agreement involving Ukrainian neutrality in exchange for a Russian withdrawal. But according to Turkey and the former head of the German Armed Forces, the peace agreement was again sabotaged by the United States and Britain, which wanted to wage war against Russia using Ukrainians. The strategy of provoking greater Russian involvement in Ukraine was one of the recommendations in a 2019 RAND report, commissioned by the U.S. military, on how Russia could be weakened.

The U.S. Secretary of Defense declared that the goal of the war was to weaken Russia. Senator Mitch McConnell confirmed that “cold, hard, practical American interests” were the reason for weakening and defeating Russia. Senator Lindsey Graham explained that the United States has a good deal because it sends weapons while Zelensky promises that “they will fight to the last person.”

If this was an unprovoked and opportunistic invasion, weapons shipments could cause Russia to withdraw because the costs would become greater than the benefits. But if Russia considers NATO an existential threat, weapons shipments will only escalate the conflict toward nuclear war. Instead of using Ukraine as a pawn in the new Cold War, we should support negotiations that provide the security guarantees Moscow demanded a year ago, based on existing agreements from the 1990s that we abandoned.

item.title: How Explaining Russia’s Motivations Became Taboo in the West
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Narrative control has seemingly rendered our societies incapable of distinguishing between ‘explanation’ and ‘justification’. There is overwhelming evidence that Russia has considered NATO expansionism to be the main security threat since the end of the Cold War, and that Russia has considered NATO’s incursion into Ukraine to be an existential threat. Yet, our political-media establishment smears and censors any explanation as “justification”. By doing so, they also criminalise any path toward a political settlement to end the war.

Germany invaded my country, Norway, during World War II to a large extent as a pre-emptive move. Britain considered invading Norway to control its Atlantic coastline, to disrupt the iron supplies that were vital to Germany, and to have a northern flank against the Germans. Norway was neutral, yet its neutrality could not be enforced as the British Navy operated in Norwegian waters without its permission. Am I ‘justifying’, “legitimizing”, or “excusing” Nazi Germany’s invasion of Norway by stating these historical facts to explain how states compete for security? To understand how our societies are abandoning strategic thinking, freedom of speech, diplomacy and peace, it is imperative to understand how our political-media establishment suppresses reality to protect war narratives.

The Western war narrative is structured around the absurd claim that the Russian invasion of Ukraine was “unprovoked”. This narrative is protected by smears and intimidation against anyone who discusses the role of NATO expansionism. The former US ambassador to Russia, who later became the Director of the CIA, wrote in 2008 that any effort to pull Ukraine into the NATO orbit could trigger a civil war in Ukraine and that “Russia would have to decide whether to intervene; a decision Russia does not want to have to face”. This is a far cry from the claim of an “unprovoked” Russian invasion to restore the Soviet Union. At the end of the first day of the Russian invasion, Zelensky confirmed that they had been contacted by Moscow to discuss putting an end to the war, which would be based on restoring Ukraine’s neutrality. Three days later, Moscow and Kyiv agreed to start peace talks that were linked to restoring Ukraine’s neutrality. This is absent from our media, as it does not fit the narrative of an “unprovoked” invasion.

After the Istanbul talks failed, we were informed by the Turkish and Israeli mediators that Russia and Ukraine were close to a deal based on restoring Ukraine’s neutrality before the US and UK decided to torpedo the agreement as they saw an opportunity to use Ukrainians to fight and weaken Russia. As Zelensky recognised in an interview with The Economist in March 2022: “Everyone has varied interests. There are those in the West who don’t mind a long war because it would mean exhausting Russia, even if this means the demise of Ukraine and comes at the cost of Ukrainian lives”. However, the only acceptable discourse in the West must seemingly be based on the premise that NATO is simply an altruistic actor that responded to Ukraine’s desire to join NATO, even though every poll between 1991 and 2014 demonstrated that only a tiny minority of Ukrainians wanted NATO membership.

The discourse is dumbed down to the extent that claiming the Russian invasion was unprovoked is the litmus test for being “pro-Ukraine,” while any dissent is labelled “pro-Russia”. Why? The situation for Ukraine has consistently worsened since 2014, and continuing along this path could destroy Ukraine as a nation. In contrast, if we recognize that Russia will not accept NATO in Ukraine any more than the US would accept the Russian military in Mexico, then a deal could be made that would manage the security competition, remove Ukraine from the front lines of a divided Europe, and create a stable and prosperous Ukraine. Yet, even discussing the possibility of reducing the security competition is criminalized as “justifying”, “legitimizing”, and “excusing” the Russian invasion.

The West has subsequently trapped itself in narratives that make peace impossible to pursue in a war it cannot win.

item.title: The Old World Order Is Collapsing | Iran, Russia & the Rise of Multipolarity
item.description: The world is entering a dangerous transition from U.S.-led unipolarity to a multipolar international order.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
The world is entering a dangerous transition from U.S.-led unipolarity to a multipolar international order. In this episode of The Golden Fleece, Lasha Kasradze is joined by Professor Glenn Diesen and Professor Pascal Lottaz to examine what this historic shift means for Iran, Russia, Europe, NATO, Georgia, and the future of global security.

Topics covered:
• The end of the unipolar world order
• The rise of multipolarity
• Iran and the Strait of Hormuz
• U.S.–Iran escalation risks
• Russia, Ukraine and NATO
• Georgia and the politics of neutrality
• Europe’s changing geopolitical role
• The decline of diplomacy
• The future of the international system

item.title: The West on the Path to World War
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
The most important question of social systems is what creates order by managing competing interests? In international security, we must therefore ask the question: How do we manage the competing security interests of states?

We have not asked this question in a long time as the post-Cold War world order was organised around the collective hegemony of the West. A hegemonic system does manage competing security interests of states, rather it seeks stability, order and peace through dominance. However, that hegemony is now gone and we must yet again address competing security interests of states.

Hegemony as Universal Values

Discussing the security concerns of other states is especially difficult for a former hegemon as it is perceived as a betrayal of universal values. Hegemons always seek to legitimise their dominance as a common good, which is why the particular interests and priveliges of the hegemon are depicted as “universal values”. The West no longer speaks about international security as competing security interests, but as universal values.

The post-Cold War world order of liberal hegemony portrayed the collective hegemony of the West as a “force for good” by allegedly advancing liberal democratic values. The Western political class raised over the past decades fully embraced an ideology based on Fukuyama’s theory of the “End of History”, as the world would unify under liberal democracy and Western leadership. Liberal hegemony became a hegemonic norm as these universal values could only prevail under Western dominance.

Predictable Actions By a Declining Hegemon

A declining hegemon will predictably seek to weaken rising powers, and all “universal values” that no longer sustains hegemony can be thrown out the window. What is the predictable response by the former hegemon?

The predictable response would be an economic war against China to prevent its technological and economic rise, and if that does not work, escalate to an actual war. In Europe, hegemony can be restored with NATO expansionism and proxy wars to weaken Russia as a rival power. In the Middle East, Iran would be the principal target for regime-change or destruction as the main rival power in the Middle East. The Western Hemisphere must again fall under the Monroe Doctrine, Africa will become a battleground for influence, and allies of the hegemon must pay tribute.

However, the hegemony is already gone. China can resist economic coercion, Russia can balance NATO expansionism, Iran has triumphantly defeated the US, and the imperial overstretch of Washington has now accelerated far beyond what is sustainable. There are no solutions to the coming economic crisis that can rescue the situation.

Thinking About Peace in a Multipolar World

Can peace only exist if the US economy and technology dominate China? Can peace in Europe only exist if NATO expansionism persists and it can attack other states unhindered? Can peace in the Middle East only exist if every rival state of the West in the region is regime-changed or destroyed? Can peace and order only exist if the West can intrude into the domestic affairs of other states?

Ask the ideological fundamentalists in the West about what creates order, and the response will always refer to some form of “universal values” linked to Western hegemony.

Our greatest challenge in the West is to adjust to a new international distribution of power: How do we achieve peace and order in a post-hegemonic world?

The West Will Choose War

Abandoning hegemonic ideologies and yet again developing systems that manage competing security interests is not easy. The new political class rose over the past decades on the belief that they had a unique role in history—they were responsible for the transition from the formerly disorderly world to a more benign, just, and stable world. In a virtuous new civilising mission, the West would dominate in perpetuity, and it would be to the benefit of all mankind. Instead, they are presiding over an era that ends 500 years of Western dominance.

In such an environment, ideological fundamentalists in the West will refuse to discuss adjusting to the new international distribution of power. They will certainly not discuss the security concerns of rival states, which is perceived as betraying universal values. Instead, we see that militant hawks rise quickly if they can promote the delusion that one great war can restore the golden era.

As the West prepares itself for perpetual war with the promise of delivering perpetual peace, the rules that legitimised the hegemon will be sacrifised. Freedom of speech, freedom of navigation, the rules of international financial system, international trade, and other rules that ensured an open and connected world are being burned down. What were sacred principles are abandoned with the support of jihadist groups, fascist groups and by even making genocide acceptable. Diplomacy is dismissed as appeasement and even the fear of nuclear war is casually dismissed as giving in to nuclear blackmail.

By rejecting a system that seeks order and peace by managing competing security interests, the West has chosen war to restore its unattainable hegemonic peace.
